en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Requiring Confession (Pāṭidesanīyakaṇḍa)
3. The Third Training Rule on Confession (Pāṭidesanīya) At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, there was a certain family in Sāvatthī that was devoted on both sides.

He prospers through faith but declines in wealth. Whatever fresh or cooked food arises in that family before the meal, he distributes it all to the monks; sometimes they remain there without having eaten at all.
People grumble, complain, and spread it about, saying:
"How can these Sakyan-son ascetics, failing to know moderation, accept [alms]?"
“Having given these things to them, they sometimes remain without food.
The monks heard those people complaining, grumbling, and lamenting.
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma on this occasion and in this context, addressed the bhikkhus:

“I allow you, bhikkhus, to grant the authorization for training (*sekkhasammuti*) by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and a second resolution (*ñattidutiyakamma*) to such a family as one whose faith increases while its wealth decreases.
And in this way, bhikkhus, it should be granted.”
A competent monk who knows the matter should inform the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
This family named so-and-so is increasing in faith but decreasing in wealth.”
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha grant the authorization for training (sekkhasammuti) to the family of such-and-such a name.
This is the motion.
Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me.
The family named so-and-so is increasing in faith but decreasing in wealth.
The Sangha grants the authorization for training to this family.
Whoever among the venerable ones approves of granting the authorization for training to this family named so-and-so, let him be silent.
"Whoever does not approve may speak.
The Saṅgha has granted the authorization for training (sekhasammuti) to the family of such-and-such a name.
It is approved by the Saṅgha; therefore, it is silent. Thus do I understand this."
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:

"Whatever families have been designated as 'in training,' if any monk, having personally accepted with his own hand hard food or soft food from such families designated as 'in training,' should chew or consume it, [he commits an offense]."
That bhikkhu should confess it thus:
“Friend, I have fallen into a blameworthy, unseemly, and confessable offense; I confess it.
In this way, this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus.
Now at that time, there was a festival in Sāvatthī.
People were inviting monks and feeding them.
That family, too, invited the monks.
Being afraid of wrongdoing, the monks did not consent,
saying, "The Blessed One has prohibited receiving fresh or cooked food with one's own hands from families designated as 'in training' and then eating it.
They complained, grumbled, and spread it about:
“What is the point of our lives if the noble ladies do not accept [offerings] from us?
The monks heard those people grumbling, complaining, and expressing their indignation.
Then the monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma on this occasion and in this connection, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, bhikkhus, when invited, to receive hard food or soft food with your own hands from families designated as ‘in training’ and eat it.
And thus, bhikkhus, you should recite this training rule:”
“Now, regarding those families designated as ‘in training,’ if any bhikkhu,
having not been previously invited, should with his own hand accept and eat or consume fresh or cooked food from such families designated as ‘in training,’ that bhikkhu must confess it thus:”
“‘Friend, I have committed an offense that is blameworthy, unbecoming, and one requiring confession; I confess it.
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, a certain monk was a regular visitor to that family.
Then, in the morning, that bhikkhu dressed, took his bowl and robe, and approached that family; having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Now at that time, that bhikkhu was ill.
Then those people said this to that bhikkhu:
“Eat, venerable sir.
Then that bhikkhu,

being scrupulous because he thought, “The Blessed One has prohibited one who is not invited from eating hard or soft food by receiving it with his own hand at families designated as ‘in training,’” did not accept it.
He was unable to go for alms;
his meal was cut off.
Then that bhikkhu went to the monastery and reported this matter to the bhikkhus.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with reference to this cause and this occasion, addressed the monks:
“I allow you, monks, when a monk is ill, to receive hard food or soft food with his own hand from families designated as ‘in training’ and to eat it.”
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus:
“Now, whatever families are recognized as ‘in training,’ if any monk, not previously invited, being not ill,
should with his own hand accept solid food or soft food from such families recognized as ‘in training,’ [he commits an offense].”
If he should eat it or consume it, that bhikkhu must confess:
“Friends, I have committed an offense that is censurable, unbecoming, and to be confessed; I confess it.
Now, as for those families designated as *sekkhasammata* (families under training):

A family designated as "in training" (sekkhasammata) is a family that increases in faith but decreases in wealth. For such a family, the designation of being "in training" has been granted by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and a second resolution (ñattidutiyakamma).
"Whoever," however, refers to whoever of such a kind... [and so on].
"Bhikkhu" ...
[as before] ... this is the "bhikkhu" intended in this context.
"In such families recognized as those of trainees (sekha)" means:
In such families designated as "those in training" (sekkha).

One who is "not invited" means one who has not been invited for that very day or for the following day; if he invites [the bhikkhu] when the latter enters the vicinity of the house, this is called "not invited."
"Invited" means invited for today or for tomorrow; he is said to be "invited" when one invites him without his having entered the vicinity of the house.
"Not being ill" means:
One who is able is able to wander for alms.
One who is ill is unable to wander for alms.
"Hard food" (khādanīya) means:
excluding the five kinds of cooked food, the time-limited [medicines], the seven-day limited [medicines], and the lifetime-long [medicines], the remainder is called "hard food.
"Soft food" (bhojanīya) means...
There are five kinds of food: boiled rice, cooked grain, flour, fish, and meat.
If one who is not invited and is not ill accepts [food] with the intention, "I will eat it," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya).

If one who is not invited and is not ill, having personally accepted with his own hand either solid food or soft food from one recognized as a trainee (sekkha), eats it or consumes it while perceiving that person as being recognized as a trainee, he commits an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya).
If one is in doubt regarding whether the person is recognized as a trainee...

[as above] ...if one who is not invited and is not ill, having personally accepted with his own hand either solid food or soft food from one recognized as a trainee, eats it or consumes it while perceiving that person as being recognized as one beyond training (asekkha), he commits an offense entailing confession.
If one accepts for the purpose of food that which is to be used within a watch of the day, within seven days, or for as long as life lasts, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
For every swallow, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is recognized as being approved by one beyond training, while one perceives it as being approved by one still in training, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one is doubtful that [the person] is recognized as one beyond training, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one recognizes as one recognized as beyond training someone who is indeed recognized as beyond training, there is no offense.
There is no offense—
He eats the leftovers of one who has been invited, or of one who is ill, or of one who has been invited or is ill.
Alms for others are prepared there;
they bring it out from the house and give it as a regular meal.
at the distribution of tickets,
on the fortnightly day,
and on the Uposatha day;

If one gives [food] that is to be consumed on the first day of the lunar fortnight, that which is to be consumed during the watch of the night, that which is to be consumed within seven days, or that which is to be consumed as long as life lasts, saying, "Consume this when there is a suitable occasion," it is for one who is insane.
"For one who is a first-offender.
The third training rule on confession is concluded.
